In the amusement game, the contestant needs to swing across to a floating platform on the water using a rope suspended from a high point, as shown in the figure. We simplify the contestant as a point mass with $m{=}60\mathrm{kg}$. The contestant grabs the rope and starts swinging from rest, with the rope making an angle $\alpha=53^{\circ}$ with the vertical direction. The length of the rope is $l{=}2\textrm{m}$, and the suspension point $O$ of the rope is at a height $H{=}3\mathrm{m}$ above the water surface. Air resistance and the mass of the rope are neglected, and the height of the floating platform above the water is not considered. The water is deep enough. The gravitational acceleration is taken as $g{=}10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin53^{\circ}=0.8$, and $\cos53^{\circ}{=}0.6$.

1. Find the magnitude of the tension force $F$ in the rope when the pendulum reaches its lowest point.
2. If the contestant releases the swing at the lowest point and lands on the floating platform, use the provided data in the problem to calculate the horizontal distance from the landing point to the shore.
3. If the contestant releases at the highest point of the swing and falls into the water. Let the average buoyant force of the water on the contestant be $f_{1}=800\mathrm{N}$, and the average resistance force be $f_{2}=700\mathrm{N}$, find the depth $d$ at which the contestant falls into the water.

raw_record.original_question:
In the amusement game, the contestant needs to swing across to a floating platform on the water using a rope suspended from a high point, as shown in the figure. We simplify the contestant as a point mass with $m=60\mathrm{kg}$. The contestant grabs the rope and starts swinging from rest, with the rope making an angle $\alpha=53^\circ$ with the vertical direction. The length of the rope is $l=2\mathrm{m}$, and the suspension point $O$ of the rope is at a height $H=3\mathrm{m}$ above the water surface. Air resistance and the mass of the rope are neglected, and the height of the floating platform above the water is not considered. The water is deep enough. The gravitational acceleration is taken as $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$, $\sin 53^\circ=0.8$, and $\cos 53^\circ=0.6$.

1. Find the magnitude of the tension force $F$ in the rope when the pendulum reaches its lowest point.
2. If the contestant releases the swing at the lowest point and lands on the floating platform, use the provided data in the problem to calculate the horizontal distance from the landing point to the shore.
3. If the contestant releases at the highest point of the swing and falls into the water, let the average buoyant force of the water on the contestant be $f_1=800\mathrm{N}$ and the average resistance force be $f_2=700\mathrm{N}$. Find the depth $d$ at which the contestant falls into the water.
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure, the suspension point of the rope is O, the rope length is l, the rope initially inclines toward the lower left, and forms an angle alpha with the vertical dashed line; the particle m is at the rope end. The vertical height from O to the water surface is marked as H. The water surface is horizontal, the left side is the bank, and on the right-side water surface there is a floating platform. The lowest point can be regarded as directly below O. According to the geometry in the figure, the horizontal distance from the bank to directly below O is taken as the horizontal projection l sin alpha of the initial position of the rope.

Reasoning: Given m = 60 kg, l = 2 m, H = 3 m, g = 10 m/s^2, sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6.

1. From the initial resting position to the lowest point, the descent height of the particle is l(1 - cos alpha) = 2(1 - 0.6) = 0.8 m. By conservation of mechanical energy: v^2 = 2g l(1 - cos alpha) = 2*10*2*0.4 = 16, so v = 4 m/s. Radial force at the lowest point: F - mg = m v^2 / l, therefore F = mg + m v^2/l = 60*10 + 60*16/2 = 600 + 480 = 1080 N.

2. When released at the lowest point, the particle makes horizontal projectile motion. The height of the lowest point is H - l = 3 - 2 = 1 m. The falling time t = sqrt(2(H-l)/g) = sqrt(2*1/10) = 1/sqrt(5) s. The horizontal velocity is v = 4 m/s, so the horizontal flight distance after release is vt = 4/sqrt(5) = 4sqrt(5)/5 m. The horizontal distance from the lowest point to the bank is l sin alpha = 2*0.8 = 1.6 = 8/5 m. Therefore the distance from the landing point to the bank is 8/5 + 4sqrt(5)/5 m.

3. If released at the highest point, namely the initial position, the falling height before entering the water is H - l cos alpha = 3 - 2*0.6 = 1.8 m. The kinetic energy when entering the water is mg(H - l cos alpha) = 60*10*1.8 = 1080 J. After entering the water, the resultant force obstructing the motion upward is f1 + f2 - mg = 800 + 700 - 600 = 900 N. By the work-energy relation, 900d = 1080, so d = 1.2 m.

In the amusement game, the contestant needs to swing across to a floating platform on the water using a rope suspended from a high point, as shown in the figure. We simplify the contestant as a point mass with $m=60\mathrm{kg}$. The contestant grabs the rope and starts swinging from rest, with the rope making an angle $\alpha=53^\circ$ with the vertical direction. The length of the rope is $l=2\mathrm{m}$, and the suspension point $O$ of the rope is at a height $H=3\mathrm{m}$ above the water surface. Air resistance and the mass of the rope are neglected, and the height of the floating platform above the water is not considered. The water is deep enough. The gravitational acceleration is taken as $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$, $\sin 53^\circ=0.8$, and $\cos 53^\circ=0.6$.

1. Find the magnitude of the tension force $F$ in the rope when the pendulum reaches its lowest point.
2. If the contestant releases the swing at the lowest point and lands on the floating platform, use the provided data in the problem to calculate the horizontal distance from the landing point to the shore.
3. If the contestant releases at the highest point of the swing and falls into the water, let the average buoyant force of the water on the contestant be $f_1=800\mathrm{N}$ and the average resistance force be $f_2=700\mathrm{N}$. Find the depth $d$ at which the contestant falls into the water.

Image description: In the figure, the suspension point of the rope is O, the rope length is l, the rope initially inclines toward the lower left, and forms an angle alpha with the vertical dashed line; the particle m is at the rope end. The vertical height from O to the water surface is marked as H. The water surface is horizontal, the left side is the bank, and on the right-side water surface there is a floating platform. The lowest point can be regarded as directly below O. According to the geometry in the figure, the horizontal distance from the bank to directly below O is taken as the horizontal projection l sin alpha of the initial position of the rope.

Reasoning: Given m = 60 kg, l = 2 m, H = 3 m, g = 10 m/s^2, sin 53° = 0.8, cos 53° = 0.6.

1. From the initial resting position to the lowest point, the descent height of the particle is l(1 - cos alpha) = 2(1 - 0.6) = 0.8 m. By conservation of mechanical energy: v^2 = 2g l(1 - cos alpha) = 2*10*2*0.4 = 16, so v = 4 m/s. Radial force at the lowest point: F - mg = m v^2 / l, therefore F = mg + m v^2/l = 60*10 + 60*16/2 = 600 + 480 = 1080 N.

2. When released at the lowest point, the particle makes horizontal projectile motion. The height of the lowest point is H - l = 3 - 2 = 1 m. The falling time t = sqrt(2(H-l)/g) = sqrt(2*1/10) = 1/sqrt(5) s. The horizontal velocity is v = 4 m/s, so the horizontal flight distance after release is vt = 4/sqrt(5) = 4sqrt(5)/5 m. The horizontal distance from the lowest point to the bank is l sin alpha = 2*0.8 = 1.6 = 8/5 m. Therefore the distance from the landing point to the bank is 8/5 + 4sqrt(5)/5 m.

3. If released at the highest point, namely the initial position, the falling height before entering the water is H - l cos alpha = 3 - 2*0.6 = 1.8 m. The kinetic energy when entering the water is mg(H - l cos alpha) = 60*10*1.8 = 1080 J. After entering the water, the resultant force obstructing the motion upward is f1 + f2 - mg = 800 + 700 - 600 = 900 N. By the work-energy relation, 900d = 1080, so d = 1.2 m.
